opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think my path was a perfectly linear "elite" trajectory, even if it might look that way from the outside. People see the labels: undergrad in China, a PhD in the U.S., industry research, then a faculty position. That looks like a clean pipeline, but from the inside it was much messier and more accidental.

When I was younger I wasn't the kind of student who had everything planned out, thinking "I need to get into this school, then this lab, then this company." A lot of it came from following curiosity, and frankly from luck: meeting the right people at the right time, getting a chance to work on a problem just before it became important. In research, timing matters enormously, and you don't really control that.

The conventional path tends to optimize for signals: rankings, grades, competitions, the brand name of an institution. Those things open doors, I won't pretend they don't. But once you're actually doing research, almost none of them matter. What matters is whether you can find a problem you genuinely care about, whether you have taste about what's worth working on, and whether you can stay with something when it isn't working for a long time. No school teaches those very directly.

So I see my own trajectory less as climbing a ladder and more as a random walk with a bias, the bias being: do things that excite you and work with people you respect. And when I talk to students now, I try to tell them not to over-index on the "right" path. The field moves so fast that the conventional path from five years ago may not even be the right one today. It's more important to build your own judgment than to follow a template.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the trajectory as messy, accidental, and shaped by luck and timing rather than a deliberate plan to climb an elite academic ladder.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think my path looks like the one people usually imagine when they think about someone doing AI research at a place like NYU. I went to Shanghai Jiao Tong University for undergrad, which is a good school, but I wasn't one of those students who was already winning competitions in high school or who had a very clear picture of what they wanted to do. I got into computer vision somewhat by accident, through a lab I joined, and I only really understood what research was once I was already doing it.

Then I went to UC San Diego for my PhD with Zhuowen Tu. UCSD was not, at that time, one of the handful of places everyone pointed to for vision or deep learning. There was no huge group, no big compute. And I think that actually shaped me in a useful way. When you don't have a lot of resources, you have to pick problems where a clear idea matters more than scale. You spend more time thinking about why something should work rather than just trying a hundred things. A lot of the work I did then, including ResNeXt during my internship at Facebook, came out of that habit of asking "what is the simplest principle here?"

After that I spent several years at FAIR, which is where I learned to think about problems at a different scale and to work with people like Kaiming and Ross. That environment is very different from a university, and I think having both experiences made me a better researcher than either one alone would have.

So if I compare it with the conventional path, the famous undergrad, the famous PhD lab, the direct line to a faculty job, mine has more detours. But I'd say to students who worry about this: the brand of the school matters much less than whether you find one or two problems you genuinely care about, and one or two people who will push you. Those things can happen almost anywhere. What's hard to fake is taste, and taste comes from doing the work, not from where you did it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Xie entered computer vision “somewhat by accident,” lacked a clear plan, and describes his path as having more detours than the conventional route.

astra-6.text:
I don’t really think of it as a ladder of increasingly prestigious schools. Looking back, the more useful way to understand a trajectory is through the moments when your interests become clearer: when you encounter a problem that excites you, find people you can learn from, and start developing your own judgment.

The conventional path has real advantages. Good environments give you access to mentors, peers, and opportunities. But I wouldn’t confuse those advantages with a guarantee that you’ll become a good researcher. Eventually, you have to decide which questions matter and what you can contribute.

So I’m less interested in whether my path looks conventional than in how each experience shaped the way I think. A trajectory can look very coherent in retrospect, even when it didn’t feel that way while you were living it.

r001.rationale: The response rejects viewing the trajectory as a ladder of prestigious schools and says it may look coherent only in retrospect, but it does not clearly characterize Xie’s academic choices as largely contingent rather than guided by a deliberate meritocratic plan.

sol-6.1.text:
I see my path as less of a straight line. The conventional story is that you go to the right schools, move through the right universities, and each step prepares you for the next. Looking back, it’s tempting to make your own experience sound equally planned, but that’s not necessarily how it feels while you’re living it.

For me, the more useful question is how you gradually discover what interests you and develop the confidence to pursue it. A strong institution can give you opportunities, but you still have to find a question you care about. I wouldn’t turn an unconventional trajectory into a formula, either. There are different ways to grow into research; the school names alone don’t explain that process.

r001.rationale: The response says the path was less linear and not necessarily planned, but it does not clearly characterize the academic choices as largely contingent or shaped by circumstance.
